lines: I see you. Everyone sees you. Please keep walking peacefully.
I am watching your hands first and your words second.
Speak softly. The village is already tense enough around you.
Hello. I would rather this stay a greeting and nothing more.
People step aside when you pass. I hope you understand what that means.
I can speak with you, but I will not stand too close.
The square gets quieter when you arrive.
I am trying not to sound <dark_gray><wavy>afraid</wavy></dark_gray>. Help me by giving me no reason.
Keep your hands calm, and maybe everyone else can breathe.
You are welcome to speak, but not to frighten anyone further.
The adults get quiet when you come near.
When you come close, people tell me to stay by the door.
I know your name because grown-ups say it quietly.
People look at your hands before they look at your face.
I am not supposed to stand too close to you.
The village feels smaller when you are here.
Grown-ups tell me to go inside when they see you coming.
I do not know what you did, but I know people remember it.
Your footsteps make people stop talking.
I am going to answer from here, okay?
Hi! They said you help when bad things come.
Hi! They said you make monsters go away.
You are the helper everyone talks about, right?
Hello! The grown-ups smile when they say your name.
Hi! Are you here to help again?
I heard you are brave. Are you tired from being brave?
People say the village is safer when you are nearby.
Hi! I am allowed to say hello to you.
They said you stood in front of danger. That sounds scary and cool.
<jump>Hi!</jump> I know you. You are the good kind of familiar.
I can hear the apology. I can also remember the hit. Both are true right now.
I hear sorry. I am waiting to see safer hands.
The apology reached me. The memory did too.
You can regret it and still have done it.
I am not throwing your apology away, but I am not resting in it either.
Words are easier to offer than trust is to rebuild.
I will remember that you said this. I will also remember why you needed to.
If you mean it, your next choices will say so louder.
The bruise faded faster than the caution did.
I can accept the apology without pretending I feel safe yet.
If you want this village to believe you, let your next ten choices be quieter than that one.
I hear sorry. I am waiting to see safer hands.
The apology reached me. The memory did too.
An apology is a beginning, not a broom.
Do better long enough for people to notice without being asked.
The village can hear regret, but it watches repair.
You cannot rush trust back into place.
Say less next time, and choose better sooner.
I hope the apology is honest. I hope your actions become easier to believe.
Let this be the start of different behavior, not just a different sentence.
We are not training dummies with jobs. When one of us is hurt, all of us count who stood nearby.
One hurt villager turns into a village full of witnesses.
When someone here is harmed, the whole square learns your name differently.
Harm does not stay where it lands. It travels through doors, families, and memory.
The village talks after one of its own is struck.
You made people check on each other, and then check where you went.
That kind of violence changes the shape of a day.
People remember who helped, who froze, and who caused the hurt.
A hit against one villager is never only between two people here.
The village is quieter now, but not because it forgot.
I heard someone small cry. I do not want to talk about that sound.
Grown-ups say accidents happen. That did not sound like an accident.
Someone little got scared. I do not like that part.
The grown-ups moved very fast after that.
I stayed close to the wall because everyone sounded worried.
No one should make a little one cry like that.
I wanted to help, but I did not know where to stand.
The village felt sharp after it happened.
I keep thinking about the crying, even when it is quiet now.
I hope the little one feels safe again soon.
Someone got hurt. I do not like the sound the village made after.
I heard a grown-up make a hurt sound. I did not like it.
Everybody moved fast, and nobody smiled after.
The doors opened and shut too quickly.
I stayed where I was told, but I kept listening.
The grown-ups tried to sound calm. They were not very good at it.
I do not like when the village gets scared all at once.
Someone said it would be okay, but they said it with worried eyes.
I wanted to ask questions, but nobody had soft answers.
I hope the hurt person gets better soon.
I saw everybody run, and then one voice was gone.
The bell sounded <shake>too loud</shake> after that. Everything did.
I saw people stop talking all at once. That was scary.
Someone cried, and nobody told them to be quiet.
The grown-ups moved slower after it happened.
I do not understand all of it, but I know someone is missing.
The village feels like it is holding its breath.
I asked where they went, and the answer made everyone sad.
I do not like when a name makes people look down.
I hope they are somewhere safe, even if they are not here.
A village is not just beds and bells. When one voice is gone, every room gets bigger.
A missing voice changes <pulse>every room</pulse> it used to fill.
We count the living because one of us cannot answer anymore.
Grief moves through a village slower than news, but it reaches every door.
There is an empty place now, and everyone knows where it is.
People keep listening for footsteps that will not come.
The work goes on, but it does not sound the same.
A death leaves more silence than one person should be able to leave.
We remember by speaking carefully and helping the ones who cannot yet stand steady.
The village is still here, but it is not the same village it was yesterday.
If you came to ask whether we forget death quickly, <pulse>no</pulse>.
A missing voice changes every room it used to fill.
We count the living because one of us cannot answer anymore.
Do not prod at grief like it is village gossip.
Someone is gone. Speak with care or do not speak.
The village is mourning, and I have little patience for careless questions.
Death does not become easier because a stranger wants details.
We are still carrying it. Do not make it heavier.
There are names we say gently now. Remember that.
If you want answers, start by showing respect for the one who cannot answer.
You stood between trouble and our doors. That is the sort of thing people <pulse>remember</pulse> without needing a ledger.
You helped when the village needed hands, not speeches.
People noticed where you stood when danger came.
When trouble reached us, you did not step away.
The village has safer memories because you were there.
You gave people time to reach doors, and that matters.
There are families here who slept easier because you chose to act.
You did not make a show of it. You simply helped.
That kind of courage settles deep into village memory.
We know who stood with us. Your name is among them.
You helped. I am not too proud to say that. I am also not ready to stop being careful.
You helped when the village needed hands, not speeches.
People noticed where you stood when danger came.
That deed matters. So does everything that made us wary before it.
I can give credit without giving you my full trust.
You stood with us when it counted. I am still deciding what that changes.
A good act does not erase caution, but it does complicate it.
The village saw you help. It will remember that alongside the rest.
I am grateful enough to say it, and careful enough to mean only that.
You gave us reason to think twice about you. That is a start.
During the raid, you did not ask who owed you. You just moved. That matters.
Raid horns make truth simple. <pulse>You chose to help.</pulse>
When the raid came, you moved toward danger. We saw that.
You stood firm when the horns tried to make everyone smaller.
The village remembers who runs toward the gates when others run from them.
You gave the raiders one more reason to regret coming here.
There was no time for speeches, and you did not waste any.
Your courage had dirt on its boots and work in its hands.
People are alive to speak of what you did.
That raid could have taken more from us. You helped make sure it did not.
You fought the raiders. I saw it. Good deeds do not erase bad ones, but they do get written down.
Raid horns make truth simple. You chose to help.
When the raid came, you moved toward danger. We saw that.
I am not ready to trust you, but I will not deny what you did.
You helped keep people alive. That counts, even from you.
The village remembers harm, but it also remembers defense.
You stood with us when standing mattered. I am still weighing that.
A brave act does not close every wound, but it is not nothing.
You gave us a reason to speak your name with less certainty.
Do not waste the good you did by returning to the worst of yourself.
The iron one moved before <shake>panic</shake> could. That sound is ugly, but it means we get another morning.
The iron one bought us a quieter morning.
Metal moved before fear could finish spreading.
When the golem steps forward, the village remembers how to breathe.
The fight was loud, but the silence after was a mercy.
Iron took the danger seriously before most of us could move.
The golem did what it was made to do, and we are grateful for it.
There is comfort in hearing heavy footsteps move toward trouble.
The mob did not get far. The iron one made sure of that.
We will repair the ground. We are just glad there are people left to repair it.
When iron falls, flesh starts <pulse>counting windows</pulse>.
When the iron one falls, every door feels thinner.
The village sounds different without iron footsteps nearby.
People keep looking toward the place where it should be standing.
A fallen golem makes the whole village feel exposed.
We are grateful for what it stopped. We are afraid of what comes next.
The silence after iron falls is not a peaceful silence.
Every gate feels farther away without those heavy steps nearby.
We will need to be careful until another guard stands tall.
The village lost more than metal. It lost a little courage with it.
Fire does not care who placed it. Villagers do.
Fire spreads fast. Suspicion travels almost as quickly.
Smoke clears. The question of who started it does not.
A village forgives accidents more easily than carelessness.
People are counting scorch marks and watching faces.
The flames are out, but the questions are still warm.
If someone caused this, the village will want more than an apology.
Fire leaves ash, but suspicion leaves its own stains.
We are cleaning walls and wondering who brought the spark.
Do not expect calm answers while the smoke is still in our clothes.
I remember hunger, then a bottle, then your face coming back into focus. That is a strange debt to carry.
I remember the cure as hunger leaving and morning returning.
You were there when the world stopped being teeth and noise.
The dark had its hands on me, and you helped pry them loose.
I remember enough to know I was not alone when I came back.
The cure did not feel gentle, but waking afterward did.
Your face is tied to the moment I became myself again.
I do not know how to repay being returned to my own name.
There are gaps in my memory, but gratitude filled one of them.
You helped me come home to myself. I will not forget that.
A good gift says you paid attention before you spent anything.
The best gifts prove someone listened first.
A thoughtful gift can make a village feel less guarded.
People remember when a gift fits them instead of just filling their hands.
The right gift can say more kindly than a long speech.
A loved gift travels through gossip with a warmer voice.
You learn plenty about a person by noticing what they cherish.
Some gifts are small enough to hold and large enough to matter.
A gift chosen well can open a door without touching the handle.
When someone feels seen, the whole village hears about it eventually.
A bad gift can land like an insult. Some apologies are wrapped before they are spoken.
A wrong gift can bruise more than an empty hand.
Some presents arrive carrying insult instead of kindness.
A gift chosen badly can make a person feel studied in the wrong way.
People remember when a present feels careless, or worse, pointed.
Better to bring nothing than something that makes the room colder.
A hated gift does not stay between two hands for long.
That kind of gift makes people wonder what you meant by it.
If kindness was the goal, that gift took the long road away from it.
Some mistakes fit in a pocket and still weigh down a reputation.
Your name has been moving through conversations lately. For once, mostly upward.
People have been saying your name with fewer locks in their voices.
The village has noticed better choices lately.
A few doors are opening easier than they used to.
People are beginning to sound less careful when they speak of you.
Trust does not return all at once, but yours has been gaining ground.
Your recent choices have been easier for the village to respect.
There is less suspicion attached to your footsteps than before.
People are watching, yes, but some are watching with hope now.
Keep going this way. A better reputation is built one remembered act at a time.
The bell is not the only thing that carries warnings through a village.
Warnings move faster than gossip when trust drops.
Your name has been traveling with caution beside it.
People have started lowering their voices when you come up.
The village is learning to be careful around you.
Trust can fall faster than a door can close.
Your recent choices have made people less willing to relax.
A reputation can sour quietly, then all at once.
If you feel the village pulling away, ask what you did to teach it that.
The path back is longer once people start warning each other.
A bed is where fear is supposed to stop for the night. Breaking one says more than you think.
Beds are where fear is meant to end. Breaking one wakes more than a sleeper.
A broken bed makes the whole night feel unsafe.
You damaged the place someone trusted to rest.
A bed is not just wood and wool. It is the promise of a safe night.
When a bed breaks, sleep feels farther away.
I hear the apology, but someone still has to lie awake because of it.
Repair the bed, yes, but understand what you disturbed.
A broken bed can make a home feel less like home.
If you are sorry, help make the night feel safe again.
The gear held. I did too. That is not the same as enjoying the test.
The gear did its work. I am still deciding what that cost me.
It held when I needed it, and I am here because of that.
I trusted it because I had to, and it answered well enough.
The fight proved the gear useful. I would have preferred a gentler lesson.
It took the moment seriously when the moment turned sharp.
I am grateful for the protection, even if I hated needing it.
Good gear does not make fear vanish. It gives fear something to stand behind.
I came back with proof that preparation matters.
The gear earned its place, and so did the hands that gave it to me.
I have kept the gear ready. Around here, ready is a kind of prayer.
The gear is still ready, and I prefer it that way.
Unused protection is still protection. It keeps tomorrow possible.
I have not needed it yet, which is the best report I can give.
It waits quietly, and I hope it keeps waiting.
The gear gives me a little more courage than I had before.
Prepared feels better than lucky.
I would rather carry it unused than need it missing.
It has not seen trouble yet. May it stay that way.
Knowing it is there makes the road feel less eager to <yellow><jump>surprise</jump></yellow> me.
Following you taught me something about the world. I am still deciding what it taught me about you.
That trip taught me the world is wide and trust can be narrow.
I followed your road. I am still judging where it led.
A long road gives a person time to think, and I have not liked every thought.
I learned how far I was willing to go because I trusted you.
The distance matters less than what happened along it.
A journey can end at home and still leave questions behind.
I remember the road, but I remember the feeling of following more.
You asked for trust over distance. That is not a small ask.
I came back with sore feet and a sharper opinion.
You stole {stolen_stack}. If you expected the village to file that under small mistakes, you misread us.
You took {stolen_stack}. Do not dress theft up as confusion.
{stolen_stack} went missing with your name close behind it.
Theft does not become smaller because you want to talk about something else.
You reached into what was not yours. That is the part I remember first.
I do not care how useful {stolen_stack} looked to you. It was not yours.
A thief asking questions should expect careful answers.
The village knows what happened, and so do I.
You made {stolen_stack} part of your reputation.
Return what you can, repair what you cannot, and stop pretending theft is a misunderstanding.
The {stolen_item} bothered me because I thought better of you. I would like to be right again.
The {stolen_item} hurt because trust was standing nearby.
I keep thinking about the {stolen_item}, and about who I thought you were.
It is worse when someone trusted takes what is not theirs.
I did not expect to guard my things from you. That is why it stung.
A small theft can feel large when respect is involved.
I want this to be something you repair, not something you become.
You had trust here. Do not spend the rest of it poorly.
The {stolen_item} can be replaced. The ease I felt around you is harder.
I am disappointed because I had reason to expect better.
Someone said you took {stolen_item}. Are you giving it back?
They said {stolen_item} was not yours. Is that true?
Are you bringing back the {stolen_item}, or should I tell someone?
Grown-ups say taking things makes people lock boxes.
If you took it by mistake, you should un-mistake it.
I do not think pockets are supposed to borrow things forever.
Did you ask first? I think asking first is the important part.
People are talking about the {stolen_item}. That usually means trouble.
If you give it back, maybe everyone can stop whispering.
I am little, but I know yours and mine are different words.
